#### What might happen during a typical model building process?

```{r, comment=NA, echo=FALSE, fig.width=15}
library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(v1=factor(c("Data wrangling", 
  "Data Visualization", 
                                "Data Visualization", 
                                "Data Preprocessing",
                                "Data Visualization", 
  "Model fitting","Evaluating forecast accuracy", "Tunning", "Model fitting", "Evaluating forecast accuracy", "Tunning", "Model fitting", "Evaluating forecast accuracy", "Tunning", "Model fitting","Evaluating forecast accuracy", "Tunning", "Model fitting", "Evaluating forecast accuracy", "Tunning",  "Evaluation", "Data Visualization", "Communication"
    
                                
                                ), levels=c("Data wrangling",
                                            "Data Visualization", "Data Preprocessing", "Model fitting", "Tunning", "Evaluating forecast accuracy", "Evaluation", "Communication")), v2=rep(1, 23), v3=1:23)

ggplot(df, aes(y=v2, x=v3)) + 
  geom_tile(aes(fill = v1)) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values= c("#a6cee3", "#666666", "#666666", "#666666","#666666", "#666666", "#666666", "#666666")) + 
  scale_y_discrete(labels = NULL, breaks = NULL) + labs(y = "")+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 270)) +  scale_x_discrete(labels = aes(v1)) + labs(x="") +  theme(legend.position="bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
```

 Number of series: 1

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, comment=NA, out.height="50%"}
library(tidyverse)
library(coronavirus)
coronavirus <- coronavirus %>% mutate(cases = replace(cases, which(cases<0), NA))
coronavirus <- coronavirus %>% mutate(cases = replace(cases, which(cases>800000), 800))
#confirmed <- coronavirus %>% filter(type == "confirmed")
confirmed <- coronavirus %>% 
  filter(type == "confirmed") %>%
  group_by(country, date) %>%
  summarise(cases = sum(cases)) 
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=15, fig.height=8, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(plotly)
p <- ggplot(confirmed, aes(x=date, y=cases)) + geom_line(colour=NA) +  theme(legend.position = "none")
p + geom_line(data = subset(confirmed,  country == "Norway"),color = "red") + theme(legend.position = "none") + ylim(c(0, 800)) + ylab("Sales")
```

# Three main factors 

1. Temporal Volume

2. Temporal Depth

3. Temporal Information

---

# Three main factors 

1. Temporal Volume: measures **how much data we store**

    Refers to the quantity of time-series data stored, determined by the number of time series and the number of observations (data points) in each series.

2. Temporal Depth: measures **how much of the underlying temporal behaviour and dynamics we retain**.

    How much temporal information is preserved within each time series, including its ability to capture short-term fluctuations, long-term trends, seasonality, periodicity, temporal dependencies, peaks, and structural changes.
    
3. Temporal Information: The **meaningful temporal characteristics and patterns contained in time-series** data that enable us to understand, analyse, and model its behaviour.


---


```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=15}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

set.seed(123)

n <- 240
t <- 1:n

# Series A: Trend + seasonality
series_A <- 0.03 * t +
  5 * sin(2 * pi * t / 12) +
  rnorm(n, 0, 0.8) + 200

# Series B: Trend + seasonality + irregular behaviour
series_B <- 0.02 * t +
  5 * sin(3 * pi * t / 12) +
  3 * sin(2 * pi * t / 3) +
  rnorm(n, 0, 2) + 100

# Add occasional peaks
series_B[c(45, 90, 150, 200)] <-
  series_B[c(45, 90, 150, 200)] + 100

data <- data.frame(
  time = t,
  Series_A = series_A,
  Series_B = series_B
)

data_long <- pivot_longer(
  data,
  -time,
  names_to = "series",
  values_to = "value"
)

ggplot(data_long, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~series, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## From observations to mental fingerprints

## How we mentally summarise a time series?

---
class: center, middle

### Our brain does not memorise every observation.

### It extracts meaningful characteristics and creates a mental representation.


---

## Mental Temporal Fingerprint

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
mental_fingerprint <- data.frame(
  Characteristic = c(
    "Trend",
    "Seasonality",
    "Variability",
    "Extreme events",
    "Periodicity",
    "Noise"
  ),
  `What we capture` = c(
    "Increasing / Decreasing / Stable",
    "Present / Absent; Weak / Strong",
    "High / Low",
    "Present / Absent",
    "12 observations",
    "High / Low"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(
  mental_fingerprint,
  format = "html",
  # caption = "Mental Temporal Fingerprint",
  align = c("l", "l")
) |>
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )
```

---
## We do not remember every observation. We remember the characteristics that describe the behaviour of the time series.

## **Can we teach computers to do the same?**

# Time series features

- **Cognostics**: **Co**mputer-aided dia**gnostics** (John W. Tukey, 1985)

- Characteristics of time series

- Summary measures of time series


**Basic Principle**

- Transform a given time series $y=\{y_1, y_2, \cdots, y_n\}$ into a feature vector $F = (f_1(y), f_2(y), \cdots, f_p(y))'$. 


---

.pull-left[
#### Time-domain representation

```{r, comment=NA, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(Mcomp)
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)
library(gridExtra)
library(ggrepel)
library(png)
library(tsfeatures)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggpubr)
# Extract required series
series_id <- c("N0001", "N0633", "N0625", "N0645","N1912", "N2012")
color = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3", "#e7298a", "#66a61e", "#e6ab02")
model <- c("Random walk with drift", "NAIVE", "Random walk with drift", "NAIVE", "ETS", "SARIMA")
six_series <- lapply(M3[series_id], function(u){u$x})
p <- lapply(six_series,
function(u) {autoplot(u) + xlab("") + ylab("")}
)
for (i in seq_along(six_series))
p[[i]] <- p[[i]] +geom_line(color=color[i]) +ggtitle(series_id[i], model[i])+theme(title =element_text(size=10, face='bold'))
grid.arrange(grobs = p, ncol = 2)
```

]

--

.pull-right[

#### Time series features

- Strength of trend


- Strength of seasonality



```{r, comment=NA, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
df <- tsfeatures(six_series, c("stl_features")) %>%
  select(trend, seasonal_strength) %>%
  rename(seasonality = seasonal_strength) %>%
  replace_na(list(seasonality = 0))
df$id <- names(six_series)

df

```

]

.pull-right[


$$y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t$$

$$F_T = max \left(0, 1 - \frac{Var(R_t)}{Var(T_t + R_t)} \right)$$

$$F_S = max \left(0, 1 - \frac{Var(R_t)}{Var(S_t + R_t)} \right)$$

.pull-right[

#### Feature-domain representation

```{r, comment=NA, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
df <- tsfeatures(six_series, c("stl_features")) %>%
  select(trend, seasonal_strength) %>%
  rename(seasonality = seasonal_strength) %>%
  replace_na(list(seasonality = 0))
df$id <- names(six_series)
ggplot(df, aes(x = trend, y = seasonality)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, color = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3", "#e7298a", "#66a61e", "#e6ab02")) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 1) +
  xlab("Strength of trend") + 
  ylab("Strength of seasonality") + 
  coord_fixed() +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = id),
    colour = "black",
    size = 5,
    box.padding = unit(0.5, "lines")
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

]

```{r, comment=NA, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# Extract the time series
x <- M3[["N1912"]]$x

# STL decomposition
fit <- stl(x, s.window = "periodic")

# Plot STL decomposition
autoplot(fit) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "STL Decomposition: M3 Series N1912",
    x = "Time",
    y = "Value"
  )
```

## Which features to use? 

- The human brain does not extract every possible feature from everything it observes. 

- It selectively attends to characteristics that are relevant to the task, context and previous experience.

- For time-series representation, we can develop a similar idea: **Task-aware and adaptive temporal feature extraction.**

---
## M-competitions

The M-competitions are large-scale empirical forecasting competitions organized to evaluate forecasting methods on many real-world time series.

| Competition | Year | Main focus |
|:---|---:|:---|
| **M1** | 1982 | First large-scale forecasting competition |
| **M2** | 1993 | Forecasting across a wider range of applications |
| **M3** | 2000 | 3,003 time series; major comparison of statistical methods |
| **M4** | 2018 | 100,000 time series; statistical + machine-learning methods |
| **M5** | 2020 | Walmart retail sales; hierarchical/grouped forecasting |
| **M6** | 2022 | Financial forecasting |
| **M7** | 2024 | Financial/economic forecasting |

---

### M4 Competition Data

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=15}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(123)

n <- 100
t <- 1:n

df <- bind_rows(
  # Series 1: Level shift
  data.frame(
    time = t,
    value = ifelse(t <= 50, 10, 20) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3),
    pattern = "Level shift"
  ),

  # Series 2: Zig-zag
  data.frame(
    time = t,
    value = 10 + rep(c(-3, 3), length.out = n) +
      rnorm(n, 0, 0.3),
    pattern = "Zig-zag"
  ),

  # Series 3: Sinusoidal
  data.frame(
    time = t,
    value = 10 + 4 * sin(2 * pi * t / 20) +
      rnorm(n, 0, 0.3),
    pattern = "Sinusoidal"
  )
)

ggplot(df, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~pattern, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Value") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

## Detect Time Series Unusal Structures

**Number of Large Jumps** (`detect_jumps_all`): Counts the number of unusually large consecutive changes in a time series. A jump is identified when the **absolute difference between consecutive observations exceeds an automatically estimated threshold**, defined by the specified upper quantile (quant) of the absolute differences. 


**Zig-zag rate** (`detect_zigzag`): Measures how frequently a time series changes direction between increasing and decreasing. It is calculated as the proportion of successive non-zero first differences that have opposite signs.

  - Low value (close to 0): Few direction reversals; relatively smooth or consistent movement.
  - High value (close to 1): Frequent direction reversals; strong alternating or zig-zag behaviour.

---

Consider the time series:
$$
y = (1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4)
$$

Step 1. Calculate first differences
$$
\Delta y = (4,-3,4,-3,4,-3)
$$

Step 2. Identify directions
- Positive (+): Increasing
- Negative (−): Decreasing
Direction sequence:
$$
(+,-,+,-,+,-)
$$

Step 3. Count direction reversals: Every change from positive to negative or negative to positive is a reversal. Here, there are 5 reversals.

$$
\text{Zig-Zag Rate} =
\frac{\text{Number of direction reversals}}
{\text{Number of successive direction comparisons}} = \frac{5}{6-1} = 1
$$
---

Another example
Consider:
$$
y = (1,2,3,4,5,6,7)
$$

Direction sequence:
$$
(+,+,+,+,+,+)
$$

There are zero reversals.
$$
\text{Zig-Zag Rate} = \frac{0}{5}=0
$$
---

## 

```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(knitr)

zigzag_interpretation <- data.frame(
  `Zig-Zag Rate` = c(
    "0.00",

    "0.21–0.40",
    "0.41–0.60",
    "0.61–0.80",
    "0.81–1.00"
  ),
  Interpretation = c(
    "No direction reversals",
```

### Other features

`jump_score_sd`: The ratio of the maximum absolute difference to the
standard deviation of first differences.  Measures the size of the largest absolute change relative to the standard deviation of absolute consecutive differences.

`jump_score_mean`: The ratio of the maximum absolute difference to the
mean of first differences.  Measures the size of the largest absolute change relative to the mean of absolute consecutive differences.

`max_abs_diff`: Calculates the largest absolute difference between consecutive observations in a time series.

`andomness_ratio_gam`: Measures the proportion of variation in a time series that remains unexplained after fitting a smooth nonlinear trend using a GAM.

`sd_diff`: Calculates the standard deviation of consecutive differences.

# tsstructure package

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("thiyangt/tsstructure")
library(tsstructure)
```
---

```{r, echo=FALSE}
set.seed(123)
# -----------------------------
# 1. Generate 100 time series
# -----------------------------
n_series <- 100
n_time <- 120
time <- seq_len(n_time)

zigzag_ids <- 1:8
jump_ids   <- 9:16
sine_ids   <- 17:24

series_list <- vector("list", n_series)
metadata <- data.frame(
  series_id = sprintf("series_%03d", seq_len(n_series)),
  pattern = character(n_series),
  n = rep(n_time, n_series),
  jump_position = rep(NA_integer_, n_series),
  jump_size = rep(NA_real_, n_series)
)

for (i in seq_len(n_series)) {
  level <- rnorm(1, mean = 20, sd = 5)
  slope <- runif(1, min = -0.05, max = 0.08)
  noise_sd <- runif(1, min = 0.8, max = 2.8)
  noise <- rnorm(n_time, mean = 0, sd = noise_sd)
  trend <- slope * time

  if (i %in% zigzag_ids) {
    # Strong alternating up/down movement
    amplitude <- runif(1, 3, 6.5)
    y <- level + trend + amplitude * (-1)^time + 0.4 * noise
    metadata$pattern[i] <- "zigzag"

  } else if (i %in% jump_ids) {
    # One large sudden level shift
    jump_at <- sample(30:90, 1)
    jump_size <- sample(c(-1, 1), 1) * runif(1, 8, 18)
    y <- level + trend + noise
    y[(jump_at + 1):n_time] <- y[(jump_at + 1):n_time] + jump_size
    metadata$pattern[i] <- "large_jump"
    metadata$jump_position[i] <- jump_at + 1L
    metadata$jump_size[i] <- jump_size

  } else if (i %in% sine_ids) {
    # Clear sinusoidal pattern
    period <- runif(1, 18, 42)
    amplitude <- runif(1, 4, 8)
    phase <- runif(1, 0, 2 * pi)
    y <- level + trend +
      amplitude * sin(2 * pi * time / period + phase) +
      0.4 * noise
    metadata$pattern[i] <- "sine"

  } else {
    # Ordinary simulated series: trend + AR(1) noise;
    # a subset has only weak seasonality.
    phi <- runif(1, 0.1, 0.8)
    innovations <- rnorm(n_time, 0, noise_sd)
    ar_noise <- numeric(n_time)
    ar_noise[1] <- innovations[1]

    for (j in 2:n_time) {
      ar_noise[j] <- phi * ar_noise[j - 1] + innovations[j]
    }

    y <- level + trend + ar_noise

    if (runif(1) < 0.25) {
      period <- runif(1, 20, 60)
      weak_amplitude <- runif(1, 0.3, 1.5)
      phase <- runif(1, 0, 2 * pi)
      y <- y + weak_amplitude * sin(2 * pi * time / period + phase)
    }

    metadata$pattern[i] <- "normal"
  }

  series_list[[i]] <- as.numeric(y)
}

stopifnot(length(series_list) == 100)
stopifnot(all(lengths(series_list) > 20))

# Long-format data frame: one row per time point
series_data <- data.frame(
  series_id = rep(metadata$series_id, each = n_time),
  time = rep(time, times = n_series),
  value = unlist(series_list, use.names = FALSE)
)
feature_names <- c(
  "max_abs_diff",
  "sd_diff",
  "jump_score_sd",
  "detect_jumps_all",
  "detect_zigzag",
  "jump_score_mean",
  "randomness_ratio_gam",
  "randomness_ratio_loess"
)
```

```{r}
series_list
```

## Computing with `tsstructure` Package

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tsstructure)
feature_df <- tsstruct(
x =  series_list,
features = c("max_abs_diff", "sd_diff", "jump_score_sd", 
"detect_jumps_all", "detect_zigzag", "jump_score_mean", "randomness_ratio_gam",
"randomness_ratio_loess"))
X <- feature_df[, feature_names, drop = FALSE]
X
```

```{r}
X
```

## Principle Component Analysis

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

# PCA cannot use missing/infinite values. Median-impute any such values.
for (nm in names(X)) {
  bad <- !is.finite(X[[nm]])
  if (any(bad)) {
    good_values <- X[[nm]][!bad]
    replacement <- if (length(good_values)) median(good_values) else 0
    X[[nm]][bad] <- replacement
  }
}

# Remove features with zero variance before scaling.
keep <- vapply(X, function(z) stats::sd(z) > 0, logical(1))
if (sum(keep) < 2) stop("At least two non-constant features are needed for PCA.")

pca_fit <- stats::prcomp(X[, keep, drop = FALSE],
                         center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

pca_scores <- data.frame(
  series_id = metadata$series_id,
  pattern = metadata$pattern,
  PC1 = pca_fit$x[, 1],
  PC2 = if (ncol(pca_fit$x) >= 2) pca_fit$x[, 2] else 0
)
pca_variance <- data.frame(
  component = paste0("PC", seq_along(pca_fit$sdev)),
  standard_deviation = pca_fit$sdev,
  proportion_variance = pca_fit$sdev^2 / sum(pca_fit$sdev^2),
  cumulative_variance = cumsum(pca_fit$sdev^2 / sum(pca_fit$sdev^2))
)
pca_variance
```

#### What if a time series contains a mixture of multiple temporal patterns?

```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)

n <- 180
t <- 1:n

# Level shift
level <- ifelse(t <= 60, 10, 15)

# Zig-zag pattern
zigzag <- ifelse(t <= 60, 0,
                 ifelse(t <= 120,
                        rep(c(-2, 2), length.out = 60),
                        0))

# Sinusoidal pattern
sinusoidal <- ifelse(
  t > 120,
  3 * sin(2 * pi * (t - 120) / 20),
  0
)

# Small random noise
noise <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.25)

# Combined series
y <- level + zigzag + sinusoidal + noise

df <- data.frame(t, y)

# Plot
ggplot(df, aes(x = t, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Time Series with Multiple Temporal Patterns",
    subtitle = "Level shift, zig-zag pattern and sinusoidal pattern",
    x = "Time",
    y = "Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```
---
class: center, middle

### How can we identify, represent, and store multiple temporal behaviours within a single time series without losing its temporal information?

---
Instead of maintaining one prototype for an entire time series, maintain prototypes for individual windows.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=15}
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)

# Generate time series
n <- 180
t <- 1:n

y <- c(
  10 + rnorm(60, 0, 0.3),
  15 + rep(c(-2, 2), length.out = 60) + rnorm(60, 0, 0.3),
  15 + 3 * sin(2 * pi * (1:60) / 20) + rnorm(60, 0, 0.3)
)

df <- data.frame(time = t, value = y)

# Define windows
window_size <- 30
step_size <- 20

windows <- data.frame(
  start = seq(1, n - window_size + 1, by = step_size)
)

windows$end <- windows$start + window_size - 1
windows$window <- paste0("W", seq_len(nrow(windows)))

# Plot
ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    data = windows,
    aes(
      xmin = start, xmax = end,
      ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
      fill = window
    ),
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = df,
    aes(time, value),
    colour = "steelblue",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = windows,
    aes(x = (start + end) / 2, y = Inf, label = window),
    vjust = 1.5,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Window-based Time Series Feature Extraction",
    x = "Time",
    y = "Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(knitr)

prototype_components <- data.frame(
  Component = c(
    "Representative Pattern",
    "Feature Fingerprint",
    "Feature Distribution",
    "Forecasting Profile",
    "Performance Profile",
    "Information Preservation Profile"
  ),
  Description = c(
    "Representative time series or reconstructed temporal shape",
    "Trend, seasonality, variability, ACF, zig-zag rate, jumps, noise, etc.",
    "Typical values, ranges and variability of features among similar time series",
    "Forecasting models that perform well, moderately or poorly",
    "Forecast accuracy measures such as MASE, sMAPE and RMSE across different horizons",
    "Reconstruction error, feature preservation and temporal similarity"
  )
)

kable(
  prototype_components,
  caption = "Components of a Temporal Pattern Library",
  col.names = c("Component", "Information Stored"),
  align = c("l", "l")
)
```

---
## Temporal Prototype Library?

- Reduce the need to store and process every individual time series.

- Preserve important temporal characteristics through representative patterns.

- Identify similar time series across different domains.

- Support efficient retrieval and clustering.

- Understand which forecasting models perform well for different temporal behaviours.

- Identify unusual or previously unseen temporal patterns.
